clue.text: Like his rights, less slender as the years go by

definitions.meaning: a person living on land without title can, after enough years, claim it under the legal doctrine of adverse possession, known by this occupier's name
the comparative of squat, short and thick, so stockier

explanation.surface: Someone's entitlements, and their waistline, both grow as time passes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as the years go by' belongs to both readings: such a claim to land matures with years of occupation, and people thicken with age.
explanation.definitionFit: Squat means short and thickset, so its comparative describes someone stockier; separately, the land occupier's legal claim bears this name.

clue.text: Maybe not quite the answer to a division exercise

definitions.text: Maybe not quite the answer to a division exercise

parts.words: Maybe not quite the answer to a division exercise
parts.note: the result of dividing one number by another, which may leave a remainder so is not the whole answer

explanation.surface: A teacher marking a pupil's long-division sum as slightly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' points to a remainder: the whole-number result of a division is the full answer only when nothing is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: In arithmetic the quotient is the number obtained by dividing one number by another.

clue.text: Ps This is no impetuous way to act

definitions.meaning: a postscript, a line added to a letter after signing

definitions.text: This is no impetuous way to act
definitions.meaning: acting on a later reflection, not on impulse

explanation.surface: A postscript to a letter warns against acting rashly.
explanation.walkthrough: A PS is something added once the letter is finished; acting on later reflection is the opposite of impetuous.
explanation.definitionFit: A postscript is something added later, and an action taken on later reflection is not impulsive.

clue.text: Thanks to the French, getting a girl is a battle

parts.note: ta is informal British for thanks
la is the French feminine word for the
Vera is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Thanks to some French people, a young woman ends up in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: TALAVERA, 1809, was a battle of the Peninsular War in Spain won by Wellington's army.
explanation.definitionFit: Talavera de la Reina in Spain was the site of a Peninsular War engagement in 1809.

clue.text: In the Army the police get the birds!

definitions.meaning: British military police, named for their red cap covers
a regional name for goldfinches, which have red faces

explanation.surface: Army police officers manage to catch some birds.
explanation.walkthrough: British military policemen are nicknamed for their red caps; the same name is an old word for goldfinches.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal Military Police wear red-topped caps, and goldfinches, with their red faces, share the nickname.

clue.text: Lady Macbeth wished she could — the tyrant!

definitions.text: Lady Macbeth wished she could — the tyrant!

parts.words: Lady Macbeth wished she could — the tyrant!
parts.note: she cried 'Out, damned spot!', wishing to remove a stain, read as a verb meaning remove a spot

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Lady Macbeth longs to get rid of a cruel ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for an absolute ruler splits as DE-SPOT, to remove a spot, which Lady Macbeth wished she could do to her bloodstained hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is a ruler with absolute and usually cruel power.

clue.text: The author gets an embrace and nothing more

parts.note: a hug is an embrace
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A writer receives a cuddle and nothing else.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor Hugo wrote Les Miserables.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Hugo was the French novelist who wrote Les Miserables.

clue.text: Unpopular watering places

parts.note: watering places are usually spas or pubs, here small sacs of watery fluid on the skin that nobody wants

explanation.surface: A guidebook's verdict on spa towns nobody visits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'watering places' suggests spas or resorts; here they are swellings full of fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: Blisters are fluid-filled bubbles under the skin, unwelcome to anyone.

clue.text: Net value comes out in the end

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase emerge in a fresh order, as something comes out differently

explanation.surface: An accountant reports that the net value is revealed only at the close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes out' rearranges NET VALUE. The adjective means happening in the end, as in 'the eventual winner'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eventual occurs finally, after a sequence of events, so it is what happens at last.

clue.text: Does it shoot round the race-track ?

definitions.text: Does it shoot round the race-track ?

parts.words: Does it shoot round the race-track ?
parts.note: two readings: a make of revolver fires rounds, and a young male horse races round a course

explanation.surface: A question about a gun being fired at a horse-racing meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shoot round' doubles as firing a round of ammunition and as racing fast round a track; the name serves both a famous revolver and a young male horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Colt is a well-known American revolver brand, and the same word means a young male horse, often raced.

clue.text: Theirs is a free-for-all policy

parts.note: free-for-all is read literally as setting everyone free, the aim of those who abolished slavery

explanation.surface: A dig at a party whose policy is a chaotic scramble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free-for-all' normally means a disorderly brawl; here it means liberty for everybody.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberators who free slaves or the oppressed pursue freedom for all people.

clue.text: Pages of railway lines ?

parts.note: pages are attendants carrying a bride's or monarch's long robe, while railway tracks carry locomotives

explanation.surface: A question about pages of a railway timetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pages' looks like sheets of a book but means young attendants who carry the trailing robe; railway lines literally bear trains.
explanation.definitionFit: Attendants who carry the long trailing part of a ceremonial robe or wedding dress are given this name.

clue.text: It can be pretty full of fish

definitions.text: It can be pretty full of fish

parts.words: It can be pretty full of fish
parts.note: recalls the idiom 'a pretty ___ of fish', meaning a mess, while also describing a pot that holds fish

explanation.surface: A remark about a container brimming with fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a pretty kettle of fish' is an old idiom for an awkward muddle; 'pretty' is here the idiom's ironic word, not 'quite'.
explanation.definitionFit: A kettle is a vessel for boiling, and the idiom 'a pretty kettle of fish' names one holding fish.

clue.text: What the low-paid miner gets ?

parts.note: a meagre wage, with the word's opening syllable sounding like the shaft where a miner works

explanation.surface: A question about the scant wages of a coalminer.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a tiny payment begins with PIT, the coal mine, so it suits a miner in particular.
explanation.definitionFit: A pittance is a very small sum of money, the sort of pay a poorly paid worker receives.

clue.text: Seat of Empire

definitions.meaning: a low upholstered couch or footstool without back or arms
describing the Turkish empire that lasted from about 1300 to 1922

explanation.surface: A phrase naming an imperial capital or throne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat of Empire' reads as one phrase for a capital city; split it into a piece of furniture and the adjective for the Turkish empire.
explanation.definitionFit: An ottoman is a padded footstool or couch, and the Turkish empire founded by Osman bears the same adjective.

clue.text: It's unusual to be out of it

definitions.text: It's unusual to be out of it

parts.words: It's unusual to be out of it
parts.note: the idiom 'out of the ___' means unusual, so being outside this word is to be unusual

explanation.surface: A remark that it is odd to be dazed or excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of it' reads as dazed; but 'out of the ordinary' is the idiom for unusual.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary means commonplace, and something 'out of the ordinary' is remarkable.

clue.text: Artisans who are new union members ?

definitions.meaning: skilled woodworkers who make fittings and furniture
people who sign up to a trade union or club for the first time

explanation.surface: Skilled craftsmen are the latest recruits to a trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both carpenters and people who join something, such as a union.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpenters who make door frames and cabinets are called joiners, and anyone who signs up to a body joins it.

clue.text: Radio can upset an islander

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A radio broadcast may annoy someone living on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges RADIO and CAN. An Orcadian comes from Orkney, the islands off northern Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Orkney, the Scottish archipelago, is called an Orcadian.

clue.text: It's just by the way

parts.note: 'by the way' suggests an aside, but literally means next to a road

explanation.surface: Someone dismissing a remark as merely incidental.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the way' normally introduces a passing comment; here 'way' is a road and the verge sits just beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The roadside is the strip of land at the edge of a road.

clue.text: Antony appealed to them for a loan

definitions.text: Antony appealed to them for a loan

parts.words: Antony appealed to them for a loan
parts.note: in Julius Caesar Mark Antony opens his speech asking the crowd, along with Romans and countrymen, to lend him their ears

explanation.surface: Mark Antony asks people to lend him money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a loan' refers to 'lend me your ears', from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony's speech opens by addressing the crowd as companions, then Romans and countrymen.

clue.text: Eve wasn't, but every woman has been since

definitions.text: Eve wasn't, but every woman has been since

parts.words: Eve wasn't, but every woman has been since
parts.note: in Genesis the first woman was made from Adam's rib, not born of parents, but every later woman was someone's female child

explanation.surface: A biblical observation about the first woman and all women after her.
explanation.walkthrough: Eve had no mother or father in the Genesis story, so she alone was never anyone's female child.
explanation.definitionFit: Every woman born has parents, so she is someone's female child; the biblical Eve was created, not born.

clue.text: Induced by a quantity of claret or port?

definitions.text: Induced by a quantity of claret or port?

indicators.note: quantity of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A question about what a good deal of wine brings on.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Induced' alone as the definition, but it is no synonym for sluggishness; the whole clue defines, since drinking much wine induces this, so it is an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: Torpor is a heavy lethargy, the drowsiness that follows drinking a lot of wine.

clue.text: The islander can go without the return half

indicators.note: one word goes outside, round the other, as 'without' meaning outside

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: half of the word return is its first three letters

explanation.surface: An island dweller can do without the return half of a travel ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go without' looks like 'do without' but uses 'without' in its old sense of outside, and 'the return half' is a ticket-sounding phrase meaning half of the word itself. Crete is the large Greek island.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Crete, the large Greek island, is a Cretan.

clue.text: It exemplifies it, grammatically

parts.note: the pronoun 'it' is the textbook example of the grammatical class that is neither masculine nor feminine

explanation.surface: A self-referential remark about a pronoun in a grammar lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'It' is the word 'it', which belongs to the grammatical class neither masculine nor feminine; the second 'it' is that class.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatical gender divides words into masculine, feminine and neither; the pronoun 'it' falls in the third class.

clue.text: Runs like this can retain the Ashes

indicators.note: like this points to the letters of the word before arranged in the shape of the answer

explanation.surface: Scoring runs like these could keep cricket's Ashes trophy for England.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the England-Australia cricket series, whose trophy is a tiny urn; 'retain the Ashes' sounds like winning but means containing cremated ashes. 'like this' rearranges RUNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Funeral vases hold cremated remains, and a small one holds the cricket Ashes.

clue.text: Prepare for a change of diet

indicators.note: the letters of the following word are changed round into a new order

explanation.surface: Get ready to alter what you eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a change of' rearranges DIET. The definition means to prepare a text for publication.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit is to revise and get a text ready for print.

clue.text: One way to get around

parts.note: 'way' is a road and 'get around' means circle, so a road that circles a town

explanation.surface: A tip on a method of travelling about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One way' suggests a method or a one-way street, and 'get around' suggests travel; read literally it is a road that circles a town centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring road is a bypass encircling a town so traffic can go round it.

clue.text: What's left doesn't look so good

definitions.meaning: on the left-hand side, the Latin sense used in heraldry

explanation.surface: The leftovers do not look appetising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's left' looks like remains; in heraldry the word means the left-hand side, from Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin for left survives in heraldry for the left side, and the everyday sense is menacing or ominous.
